Cunning
KUN-ing
adjective
From Old English cunnan, “to know, to be able,” the same root that gives us can and ken. A cunning man was simply a knowing man — one who had the skill of a thing in his hand; the sly, crafty sense came later, as knowledge was suspected of scheming.

Biblical Definition

In the KJV cunning means skilful, expert, masterly — and it is almost always praise. The modern ear hears the word and thinks of the fox: sly, crafty, underhanded. The Authorized Version means the opposite instinct: the hand that knows its work, the craftsman filled by God to do it well. When the LORD equips Bezaleel for the tabernacle He fills him with the Spirit of God “to devise cunning works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass” (Exo 31:4) — cunning here is a gift of the Holy Ghost, not a vice. David is commended as one “cunning in playing” (1Sa 16:18), a skilful harper whose music quieted a tormented king. The exile who fears to lose his art prays, “let my right hand forget her cunning” (Psa 137:5) — that is, its learned skill upon the harp. Even Esau the “cunning hunter” (Gen 25:27) is simply an expert woodsman. So the word gathers up every honest mastery: the weaver, the engraver, the musician, the smith. Scripture does know a crafty subtilty and condemns it, but it does not call that cunning. The believer should hear the word rightly and give thanks: skill of hand is no accident of nature but a stewardship from the God who fills men with wisdom to work, and it is to be laid, like the tabernacle’s gold, upon His altar.

Webster 1828 Definition

Skilful, knowing, expert; the learned skill of the hand, not slyness.

expand to see more

CUNNING, skilful; knowing; well-instructed; possessing the skill or knowledge to perform a thing.

From Old English cunnan, “to know, to be able,” kin to can and ken.

The original sense is knowledge or skill; the sly, artful sense is a later degradation.

Bezaleel devised cunning works in gold and silver and brass (Exo 31:4).

David was cunning in playing upon the harp, a skilful musician (1Sa 16:18).

Key Scripture

Exo 31:4 — "To devise cunning works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass,"

1Sa 16:18 — "Then answered one of the servants, and said, Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, that is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters, and a comely person, and the LORD is with him."

Psa 137:5 — "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning."

Gen 25:27 — "And the boys grew: and Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents."

Modern Corruption

An honest word for skill that has slid into a word for slyness — the knowing hand mistaken for the scheming heart.

expand to see more

The drift here is real but honest, and worth naming because it turns praise into suspicion. In the Authorized Version a cunning man is a skilled man; in ours a cunning man is a sly one. The change came as men learned to distrust cleverness — knowledge in another’s hands looked like advantage, and the word for skill slid over to mean the artful use of it against you. So the modern reader meets Bezaleel “cunning” in gold and hears something faintly sinister, when the text means only that God had made his hand expert. Read the word as praise and the tabernacle passages open at once: the LORD is the giver of skill, and skill offered back to Him is worship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that skill is a gift and a stewardship. Our age is quick to divorce talent from the Giver, to speak of a “natural” gift as if it rose from the man himself; Scripture will not have it. The same Spirit who raised Bezaleel to devise cunning works is the Spirit of holiness, and the hand He fills He fills for His house. The musician, the builder, the artisan owe their cunning to God and answer to Him for it. Let no man boast in the skill of his right hand, but let him remember Who taught it — and lest he forget, let him pray with the exile that his right hand may forget her cunning before it forgets Jerusalem.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means skilful and knowing, from the old root for knowing and being able.

expand to see more

Cunning — from Old English cunnan, “to know, to be able.”

Kin to can (be able) and ken (to know).

In the KJV it means skilful, expert, masterly — nearly always praise.

Bezaleel and Aholiab were cunning workmen for the tabernacle (Exo 31:4).

The sly, crafty sense is a later corruption of an honest word.

Usage

"A cunning workman in the KJV is a master craftsman, not a schemer."

"David’s cunning was in his harp-hand — skill the LORD had taught him."

"To be cunning in playing is to play well, and to God’s glory."
